title: The AI data center e-waste problem is huge — and getting bigger
content:
E-waste from the AI boom has been vastly underestimated, a new report warns. By 2050, it could become enough trash to fill 23 million shipping containers — roughly enough 40-foot containers to circle the world six times if lined up in a row.
The AI data center e-waste problem is huge — and getting bigger
AI is creating more e-waste, and most of it flies under the radar.
It’s a significantly higher estimate of AI’s e-waste than previous studies have found because the authors of the new report factor in all the infrastructure needed to support servers in data centers. The broader scope provides a clearer picture of junk AI leaves behind, according to the nonprofit Basel Action Network (BAN), which published the paper today.
”AI may feel weightless, but every model depends on an enormous amount of highly specialized, cutting edge hardware,” Jim Puckett, founder and chief of strategic direction at BAN, says in a press release. “If companies and governments do not begin planning for this new waste tsunami, today’s AI buildout could become an even more cataclysmic toxic waste crisis than we are already experiencing.”
“Today’s AI buildout could become an even more cataclysmic toxic waste crisis than we are already experiencing.”
Less than a quarter of the 68.3 million tons of e-waste created each year worldwide is formally collected and recycled. Most e-waste is ultimately dumped into shadowy “informal” waste collection where burning or burying equipment can expose workers and the local environment to toxic materials like lead and chromium.
The US, with far more data centers than any other country, has yet to ratify the Basel Convention established to limit the international trade of hazardous wastes. US recyclers still ship e-waste abroad, investigations have found, where it often slips into “backyard recycling.” Millions of children forced to work or live nearby face health threats from that informal recycling, according to the World Health Organization.
BAN predicts e-waste generated globally will triple in amount to up to 211 million metric tons a year by 2050. It attributes about 15 to 20 percent of that garbage to AI. Unlike previous AI e-waste estimates that focused on servers and GPUs, BAN expands its count to include other categories of equipment: power supply and distribution, cooling systems, backup power, and networking equipment. Notably, BAN also counts what it calls “AI Waste Contagion” — a wide-ranging category that incorporates everything from telecommunications infrastructure to personal devices likely to become obsolete and replaced earlier as a result of advances in AI.
Counting it all up, BAN expects 70,000 metric tons of e-waste per gigawatt of data center capacity. It cites a McKinsey projection of total data center capacity reaching up to 219GW by 2030.
Considering AI-related electronic equipment retired between 2025 and 2050, BAN concludes that’ll add up to between 395 to 617 million metric tons of e-waste by the middle of the century. It breaks down to about 8.6 million to 13.1 million metric tons of equipment retired each year as a result of AI.
Previous estimates of AI’s e-waste have been more conservative. But by focusing on servers and accelerators, past studies miss about 87 percent of a data center’s electro-mechanical infrastructure, according to BAN.
A separate study published in 2024 predicted that e-waste from AI could reach between 1.2 million and 5 million tons by 2030. Another study published in February found that AI servers could create between 131,000 and 225,000 tons of e-waste annually by the end of the decade — an amount that’s still comparable to all the e-waste produced by a country the size of Denmark.

report.summary: A new Basel Action Network report warns AI data center e-waste is vastly underestimated and could reach 395–617 million metric tons by 2050.
report.background: The AI boom has triggered massive construction of data centers filled with specialized servers, GPUs, cooling systems, power equipment, and networking gear. Previous e-waste estimates focused mainly on servers and accelerators, but the Basel Action Network (BAN) broadens the scope to include all supporting infrastructure and AI-driven obsolescence of other electronics. Global e-waste already totals 68.3 million tons annually, yet less than a quarter is formally collected and recycled. Much of the rest enters informal recycling, where burning and burying expose workers and communities to toxic materials like lead and chromium. The US has not ratified the Basel Convention, which limits hazardous waste trade, and US recyclers have shipped e-waste abroad. With data center capacity projected to reach up to 219GW by 2030, BAN warns the problem is accelerating.
key_points: BAN says earlier AI e-waste studies missed about 87 percent of a data center’s electro-mechanical infrastructure by counting only servers and GPUs. Its broader tally includes power supply and distribution, cooling, backup power, networking equipment, and “AI Waste Contagion” — telecom gear and personal devices made obsolete faster by AI advances.

The report estimates 70,000 metric tons of e-waste per gigawatt of data center capacity. Using McKinsey’s projection of up to 219GW by 2030, BAN calculates that AI-related equipment retired between 2025 and 2050 could generate 395–617 million metric tons of e-waste, or 8.6–13.1 million tons annually.

Global e-waste is projected to reach up to 211 million metric tons per year by 2050, with AI responsible for roughly 15–20 percent. Less than a quarter of today’s 68.3 million tons of annual e-waste is formally collected and recycled, leaving most to informal disposal.

Informal recycling often involves burning or burying equipment, exposing workers and nearby communities to lead, chromium, and other toxins. The World Health Organization says millions of children forced to work or live near such sites face serious health threats.

BAN warns that without planning by companies and governments, the AI buildout could become a “cataclysmic toxic waste crisis.” The US, which has more data centers than any other country, still has not ratified the Basel Convention limiting hazardous waste exports.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the report signals that compute growth carries a looming materials and reputation risk. Data center operators and cloud providers may face pressure to design for circularity, track hardware footprints, offer takeback, and use certified recyclers. Developers can push for efficient models, longer hardware life, and greener cloud regions, while regulators may tighten e-waste rules. For regular users, AI advances could shorten device replacement cycles, raise hidden environmental costs, and increase calls for right-to-repair and transparency. If left unmanaged, the waste burden will fall disproportionately on informal recyclers and vulnerable communities, turning AI’s benefits into a global toxic cleanup liability.
report.tools: To follow up, read BAN’s report and the Basel Convention texts; use e-Stewards or R2 certified ITAD recyclers for responsible disposal. Track digital footprints with open-source tools like Boavizta and Cloud Carbon Footprint. Support right-to-repair via iFixit, Open Repair Alliance, and Repair Café. The Green Software Foundation’s SCI specification can help teams measure and reduce AI-related emissions and hardware churn.
